headline: Gold sank about 3% to a one-year low under $3,900 as two Federal Reserve officials called for more rate hikes. The dollar still slipped, because a slide in tech shares pulled US bond yields lower.

chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: Two Federal Reserve officials, Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan and St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem, called for more rate hikes. The dollar index still fell about 0.4% to near 101.6, as a slide in tech shares kept US bond yields low.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: High oil from the US–Iran war has kept US inflation well above the Federal Reserve's 2% goal. The Fed raised rates in September, then held on Wednesday, October 28, with two officials voting to hike. What changed: Logan, who votes on rates this year, said the Fed needs at least two more quarter-point hikes and then a pause; Musalem said a hike is needed soon. US wage costs rose 0.8% in July to September, exactly as forecast, and a Chicago business survey cooled, though the prices firms pay jumped to their highest since 2021. Even so, markets trimmed the odds of a December hike to about 70%, from about 84% after Wednesday's meeting, as worries over AI spending sent money into Treasuries. What it means: The Fed's hawks are getting louder, but bond buyers are listening more to the stock slide, and lower yields cut the dollar's interest-rate edge. The question to keep asking: does the stock slide drag yields down faster than Fed officials can push them up?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: China's official factory surveys at 8:30 PM CT tonight, then the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3. US clocks go back an hour on Sunday. The October US jobs report comes next week, and the next Fed decision is December 9.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro gave back its early gains to end near $1.117 after German inflation cooled more than expected. Hot price figures from Italy and France, and faster euro-area growth, still keep a December rate hike likely.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Energy costs from the Iran war have pushed euro-area inflation to about 3.8%, and the European Central Bank has raised its deposit rate to 2.50%. On Thursday it held, and President Christine Lagarde said a hike was discussed, pointing to December. What changed: German inflation slowed to 2.8% in October from 3.3%, below the 3.1% expected, helped by a fuel tax cut. Italy's jumped to 5.4% and France's rose to 3.4%, both above forecast. The euro-area economy grew 0.4% in July to September, twice the forecast, though Ireland flattered the total, France shrank and Italy stalled. The euro rose to about $1.120 in Asia, then slipped back to about $1.117. What it means: The euro area is pulling two ways, with its biggest economy cooling while others run hot. That keeps a December hike likely but not locked in, and the euro keeps losing ground to the pound. The question to keep asking: does euro-area inflation, out Wednesday, stay near 3.8%?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the euro-area inflation flash estimate for October at 4:00 AM CT on Wednesday, November 4 (3.8% in September), after US clocks change on Sunday. France's parliament votes on the revenue part of its budget on November 3.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: The pound was the strongest major currency in European trading and ended near $1.340, while the euro fell to its weakest against the pound this year. A Bank of England survey showed firms expect faster price rises, backing a rate hike on Thursday, November 5.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, and markets see a Bank of England hike on November 5 as almost certain. Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday passed calmly. What changed: The pound rose above $1.34 in European trading and the euro fell to about 83.4 pence, its lowest this year. A Bank of England survey showed firms expect prices to rise 3.3% over the next year, up from 3.1%. Nationwide house prices were flat in October, with yearly growth the slowest since early 2024. What it means: Firms expecting faster price rises make next week's hike easier to justify, and with the Budget behind it the pound is trading on rates. It is gaining most against the euro, where growth is patchier. The question to keep asking: does the Bank of England hint at a second hike in December?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the Bank of England decision at 6:00 AM CT on Thursday, November 5 (US clocks change on Sunday). Until then, the pound mostly follows the US dollar and the global mood.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% but said underlying inflation has reached its 2% goal. Governor Kazuo Ueda then gave no date for the next hike, so the yen gave back some of its gains, ending near ¥157.5 per dollar.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Japanese rates are far below US rates, which keeps the yen weak near ¥158 per dollar, and Tokyo has warned it is ready to step in. Most economists expect the bank's next hike in December. What changed: The bank held by 8 votes to 1, with board member Hajime Takata wanting a hike, and raised its price forecast for the year to March 2028 to 2.6%. At his press conference Ueda said the goal is not fully reached and the bank will adjust as needed rather than wait, but named no date. The dollar dipped to about ¥157.1 overnight, then recovered to about ¥157.5 by the New York close. What it means: The bank has moved closer to a December hike without promising it, so the yen got only a modest lift. Falling US yields and nervous stock markets helped too, while high oil keeps costing Japan. The question to keep asking: how soon does the Bank of Japan raise rates again?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: China's factory surveys at 8:30 PM CT tonight, then the US jobs report next week. The next Bank of Japan decision is December 18.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: The franc ended near 0.824 per dollar, firmer on the day, as the slide in tech shares kept money looking for safety. Switzerland's KOF economic barometer slipped but stayed well above its long-run average.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Swiss inflation is below target and the Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero, so the franc mostly moves as a safe place for money in tense times. What changed: The KOF barometer, a gauge of where the Swiss economy is heading, fell to 107.6 from 109.1, below the 108.1 expected. The dollar touched about 0.821 francs in Asia, near a one-month low, and ended near 0.824 at the New York close, down about 0.3% on the day. What it means: The Swiss economy is cooling, not turning down, so the central bank has no reason to change rates either way. The franc's strength comes from nervous markets, and it lasts only as long as the nerves do. The question to keep asking: are investors still looking for safety?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, which could bring news on Iran, and Swiss inflation figures next week. The next Swiss rate decision is December 10.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The Aussie held near 70.4 US cents, up slightly on the day despite falling share markets. A Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike on Tuesday is still strongly expected, and China's factory surveys come tonight.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Australian inflation has run above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, and the bank has raised rates four times this year. Hot consumer price figures on Wednesday made a fifth hike, on November 3, likely. What changed: Prices businesses charge each other rose 1.1% in July to September, slightly above forecast, and private-sector borrowing grew 0.6% in September. The Aussie ended near 70.4 cents at the New York close, up about 0.1%, as a softer US dollar offset the stock slide. What it means: Price pressure still building up the supply chain backs the case for a hike next week. That rate edge is holding the Aussie up on a day when nervous markets usually hurt it. The question to keep asking: does anything talk the Reserve Bank of Australia out of a November hike?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: China's official factory surveys at 8:30 PM CT tonight (forecast 49.9, just under the 50 line between growth and decline), then the Reserve Bank of Australia decision at 9:30 PM CT on Monday, November 2, after US clocks change.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: Canada's economy did not grow in August, missing forecasts, yet the loonie rose to about 1.395 per US dollar. A jump of about 2% in US crude and a broadly weaker US dollar outweighed the soft growth.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Higher energy prices pushed Canadian inflation up, and on Wednesday the Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.50%, its first hike since 2023. Governor Tiff Macklem said more hikes are possible but the bank will move carefully. What changed: Statistics Canada said output was flat in August against a 0.2% gain expected, after a flat July, and an early estimate points to a small fall in September. That leaves growth well below the bank's forecast. The US dollar still fell about 0.3% to about 1.395 loonies as US crude rose above $104. What it means: Weak growth makes a second hike in December harder to justify, which would normally weigh on the loonie. For now, costly oil and a softer US dollar matter more. The question to keep asking: can high oil keep carrying the loonie if Canada's economy stalls?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, and any news on Iran, which moves oil. The next Bank of Canada decision is December 9.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Brent ended near $116.6 a barrel and US crude jumped about 2% to $104 on fear of new US strikes on Iran. Gulf exports have recovered, but thin stockpiles and costly shipping keep prices high.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: The US–Iran war, which began in February, has largely shut shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and kept oil above $100. US officials have warned allies to prepare for possible new strikes after the November 3 midterm elections. What changed: The Wall Street Journal reported that the head of US Central Command, Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed President Donald Trump on options that include a return to major fighting, and Brent briefly topped $117. Gulf crude exports are back above pre-war levels, with about 40% now avoiding the strait, but world stockpiles are far below pre-war levels and shipping costs are about ten times normal. What it means: Oil is priced on risk, not on flows: even with more crude moving, the threat of new fighting keeps a premium in. That helps exporters like Canada and costs importers like Japan and the euro area. The question to keep asking: does the US move toward strikes or talks after the midterms?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the OPEC+ meeting on Sunday, expected to keep December output targets unchanged, then the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, and any reply from Iran to US proposals.

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: Gold fell about 3% to near $3,880 an ounce, its lowest in a year, even as shares slid. Two Fed officials calling for more rate hikes, and selling to cover stock losses, outweighed gold's usual pull in a scare.
chapters.meaning: The story so far: Gold peaked near $5,600 in January but has slid since the Fed resumed raising rates, because higher rates make a metal that pays no interest less attractive. What changed: Gold slipped below $4,000 in Asia, then fell through $3,900 in the US session after St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said another hike is needed soon; later Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan called for at least two more. Silver fell about 6%. Analysts said some investors sold gold to cover losses on falling tech shares. What it means: Gold is trading on the Fed, not on fear: a softer dollar and lower bond yields would usually help it, but not today. It now sits about 30% below its record. The question to keep asking: do bets on Fed hikes keep rising?
chapters.fx: What's next: Coming up: the US midterm elections on Tuesday, November 3, which could bring news on Iran, and the October US jobs report next week.

calls.text: Brent near $112 after the Iran strike-plan report: a confirmed hit on Gulf oil output or a US move toward strikes pushes it above the $112.68 high and lifts the yen and franc; an official denial lets it slip toward $108 by the close
calls.note: Brent did top the high, to about $113, and the yen and franc gained, but without a confirmed hit or an official US move: the report alone and Iran's tanker claims did it.

calls.text: Euro-area consumer confidence 9:00 AM CT (about −17 expected) with France's gap over Germany at its widest since 2011: a weaker reading keeps the euro under $1.12; a steady one lets it recover
calls.note: The reading was weaker (−17.9), yet the euro recovered to about $1.1218 as US yields fell, so the bond rally outweighed the survey.

calls.text: US bond rally on war fears: if the 10-year yield stays near 5.05% into the close, the yen holds its gains near ¥157; if yields rebound on the strong claims figure, the dollar climbs back toward ¥158
calls.note: Yields did not rebound; they fell further, to about 4.95%, on a tech sell-off, and the yen extended its gains to about ¥156.85.

calls.text: US 10-year yield below 5% after the tech sell-off: if Asian and European stocks keep falling overnight, the yen pushes toward ¥156 and the dollar index slips under 101.5; a rebound in stocks lifts yields and the dollar back toward ¥157.5
calls.note: Asian stocks kept falling (Nikkei −1.3%) and the dollar dipped to about ¥156.3, but steadied near ¥156.9 by 12:40 AM CT; the dollar index held at about 101.5 rather than slipping under it.

calls.text: Euro-area flash business surveys Fri 3:00 AM CT (manufacturing ~52.7, services ~52.6 expected), hours before Moody's on France: misses keep the euro near $1.12; beats firm December ECB hike bets and lift it
calls.note: The surveys missed (euro-area composite 51.9, France back in contraction at 48.4), and the euro stayed near $1.12.

calls.text: US flash PMIs Fri 8:45 AM CT (services ~58.0 expected) and Michigan inflation expectations 9:00 AM CT: firm readings lift yields back toward 5% and steady the dollar; soft ones extend the bond rally
calls.note: The surveys were firm on prices and the Michigan inflation outlook ticked up; the 10-year yield rose back to about 5.00% and the dollar index firmed to about 101.8 on Friday.

calls.text: SNB policy summary 2:30 AM CT: worry about a strong franc keeps December cut bets alive and caps the franc; a calmer tone lets it firm
calls.note: Calmer tone: the bank dropped its stronger readiness to intervene and gave no December cut signal. The franc firmed slightly, with the dollar near 0.823, and hit a three-month high against the euro.

calls.text: Saudi departure order: widening across the Gulf or a hit on Saudi output puts Brent well above $110 and lifts the dollar and loonie; staying contained lets oil drift
calls.note: Brent did climb well above $110 (about $113 by the close), but on reports of US–Israeli strike plans and Iranian tanker claims, not a wider departure order. The loonie edged up; the dollar slipped.

calls.text: UK retail sales Fri 1:00 AM CT (−0.2% expected): a strong print lifts December hike bets and the pound; a weak one trims both
calls.note: Sales fell 0.4%, worse than expected, yet the pound reached its strongest against the euro since May 2025 on Friday as a November Bank of England hike stayed near certain.

calls.text: US jobless claims Thu 7:30 AM CT (about 200,000 expected): staying low keeps the Fed's December hike near 90%; a jump trims it and weighs on the dollar
calls.note: Claims stayed low at 194,000 (200,000 expected), near their lowest in decades. December hike bets held near 90% (CME FedWatch, Oct 21); a sharp bond rally later still pulled the dollar lower.

calls.text: Moody's review of France Fri: a downgrade widens France's gap over German yields and weighs on the euro; holding the rating eases the pressure
calls.note: Moody's held France at Aa3; French yields eased on Monday and the euro led the majors in the European morning.

calls.text: Bailey 8:00 AM CT after the 3.5% UK inflation print: backing November without promising more keeps the pound near $1.34; any opening to a December follow-up lifts it; calling energy temporary trims it
calls.note: Neither branch: Bailey gave no new signal on rates. The pound still held near $1.34 (about 1.3395 at the New York close), with December's second hike about a coin toss.

calls.text: US crude oil stocks 9:30 AM CT (industry survey: about −4.9M barrels): a big official draw keeps Brent above $110; a build lets the rebound fade
calls.note: The draw came (−3.1M barrels, far more than forecast) and Brent briefly topped $110.8, but it still faded to $108.82 at the settle after the US Treasury's tanker licence and emergency fuel loans.

calls.text: Pakistan's mediation after Iran's uranium refusal: any confirmed opening drains oil's premium and lifts the euro and yen; more warships and no talks keep Brent near $110 into the close
calls.note: No opening: Rubio called a deal extremely difficult and more US warships headed in. Brent settled at $108.82, near $110 but off its high on Washington's supply moves rather than diplomacy.

calls.text: Japan national CPI Thu 6:30 PM CT (2.1% expected): a hot print keeps the BoJ's December hike near three in four; a soft one fades it and weighs on the yen
calls.note: Neither branch: 2.1% exactly as expected (1.7% prior), though the measure that also leaves out energy jumped to 2.4%. December hike pricing held near 80%.

calls.text: US–Iran framework: confirmation by either government drains oil's risk premium and pulls US long yields lower; another denial puts Brent back toward $110
calls.note: No confirmation from either government, and no fresh denial either. Brent still climbed back toward $110 overnight, on tanker attacks spreading to the Gulf of Oman rather than on the talks.

calls.text: RBA's Hauser 5:30 PM CT: leaning on sticky inflation keeps a November hike near 1 in 3; leaning on the softer job market trims it
calls.note: Hauser leaned on sticky inflation: the outlook is 'materially worse'. Odds of a November hike rose to about 40% from about 30%, and the Aussie hit a three-week high near 0.702.

calls.text: China Q3 GDP 4.5% vs 4.4% fc — the aussie's demand read
calls.note: Beat: 4.5% vs 4.4% fc (q/q 1.2%); retail +1.1% the standout. AUD/USD +0.3-0.5% to ~0.697, the night's best G10 performer; USD/CNH 6.6811, strongest since June 2022. Two-speed beat (factories lead, property -20.6% YTD).

calls.text: Petersburg Oil Terminal drone strike — Baltic supply risk into Monday's open vs the waiver's lower-price pull
calls.note: Fire CONFIRMED (Beglov; Fire Point confirmed its FP-1 hit the terminal); ~1 killed, several injured (figures vary); damage extent still unquantified. Crude's Sunday open came flat — neither the spike nor the tumble; Asia Brent -1.0 to -1.8%.

calls.text: Beirut strike fallout: the haven-bid tell at Monday's open
calls.note: No Hezbollah retaliation as of Monday's open (Qmati: strike crossed a 'red line', leadership to decide; IDF: normal routines). Haven bid stayed sheathed — DXY flat 101.80-101.83, havens ~flat in Asia. The tell held: no escalation, no haven extension.

calls.text: October FOMC priced as a hold (~85%) into the Saturday blackout; December is the live debate
Brent broke $108 on Ukraine refinery strikes — $105-112 range into the weekend (prior $104-108 call broken)
USD/CAD holds 1.41-1.43 into the BoC (Oct 28); Canada CPI Mon the trigger
calls.note: Oct 19: CPI passed without a break — USD/CAD ~1.411 at the NY close, still inside the range. Runs to the Oct 28 decision. Oct 20: dipped to ~1.409, a hair under the floor, as oil and BoC hike bets lifted the loonie. Oct 20 close: broke below the floor — USD/CAD ~1.406, strongest loonie since Sep 22, on BoC hike pricing (~80–85%) and Alberta's vote to remain.
The tripwire never bit — Friday's waiver suspends the duties outright with no end date. Superseded by the ~Dec 17 60-day review clock.
calls.text: Graham Act Oct-18 tripwire: waivers extended or enforcement begins — oil's Sunday open is the tell
Iran deal Sunday signing: Trump's 'OPEN TO ALL' vs Tehran's 'not tomorrow' — the strait itself is the verdict
calls.note: No signed deal carried by any major wire by 4pm CT Sunday; Trump's 'complete' claim stands unverified against Tehran's 'talks stalled'. Aggregator 'markets celebrate' content held — its futures numbers contradict Friday's verified settles. The signing test is claim day, not done day.

calls.text: Canada CPI Mon 7:30am CT (TD 3.2%, UBS 3.3%, RBC 3.0%): hot (3.3%+) revives the Oct 28 hike; soft (3.0%-) buries it to December
calls.note: Neither branch: 3.1% vs 3.2% expected, core measures cooled to 1.8–1.9%. October stayed about 1 in 4 (a hold), with about one quarter-point hike priced by December; consumers' inflation expectations rose to ~3.9% in the BoC survey. Correction (Oct 20): by Monday's close swaps had jumped to ~87% for an October hike on Macklem's Saturday forecast warning; the 1-in-4 figure was stale.

calls.text: UK CPI Wed 1am CT (3.4% fc vs 3.1%): 3.5%+ starts pricing a December follow-up; soft reopens Bailey's 2027 read
calls.note: Hot branch: 3.5% vs 3.4% expected (3.1% in August), the highest in 11 months. November's hike is near certain; how much December moved was not yet verified at write.

calls.text: NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (ANZ 3.8% y/y): hot settles the RBNZ's two-way bet toward the hike side
calls.note: Not hot: inflation came in at 3.7%, a touch soft. The hike side still settled anyway, with October 28 now about 98% priced.

calls.text: Japan CPI Fri + BoJ Oct 29-30: Ueda's 'quite close' language tested — October hike stays ~25%
calls.note: Oct 19: swaps now put an October 30 hike under 5% (BBH), below the ~25% in the call. December ~80% unchanged. October hike odds fell to about 4%, far below the ~25% in the call; Japan's inflation came in at 2.1% as expected and December (~80%) is now the meeting that matters.

calls.text: France's revenue-section budget vote Tue: a clean pass narrows the French–German spread (~141bp); a defeat or big concessions widens it and weighs on the euro
calls.note: No vote on Tuesday: it was pushed to October 27, so neither branch played out.

calls.text: UK jobs Tue 1 AM CT (earnings ~3.8% expected): sticky pay firms the BoE hike case before Wednesday's inflation; cooling pay backs Bailey's calmer view
calls.note: Sticky side won: unemployment fell to 4.7% (4.9% expected) and regular pay rose 3.7% (3.6% expected); total pay and claims were softer. Pound +0.3% to ~1.334.

calls.text: Konarak follow-through: a US confirmation or more strikes keeps oil's supply premium and lifts US yields; silence lets the morning's waiver drop resume
calls.note: No confirmation (a US official denied the strike) and no new strike overnight, yet the premium held: Brent ~$109.8 Tuesday on low Gulf flows and Iran's Hormuz claims. The waiver-driven drop did not resume.

calls.text: BoC Oct 28 with ~87% priced for a hike: a hike is mostly in the loonie already; a hold would be the surprise and hit it
calls.note: The Bank of Canada hiked as priced, and the loonie barely moved on the day.

calls.text: NZ Q3 CPI Wed 4:45pm CT (~3.8% y/y): near forecast keeps the ~80% hike pricing; clearly soft reopens the hold and weighs on the kiwi
calls.note: Near forecast (3.7% vs 3.8%) and hike pricing held, rising to about 98%; the kiwi dipped only briefly.
